name: Collagen peptides

chain: Hydrolysed collagen is swallowed daily as a powder, drink or capsule
Digestion yields peptides rich in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline that reach the blood
Proponents say they signal skin cells to support hydration, elasticity and the dermal matrix, giving smoother, firmer-looking skin
angle.text: People take collagen peptides to support skin hydration, firmness and fine-line appearance from the inside, and sometimes for hair, nails and joints so they can keep training. Randomised trials of oral peptides have reported improvements in measures such as skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles, and several meta-analyses have pooled them.

infobox: Skin hydration, elasticity, wrinkle depth, bone density
lead: Collagen peptides, also called hydrolysed collagen or collagen hydrolysate, are short chains of amino acids produced by enzymatically breaking down animal collagen, usually from bovine, porcine or marine sources. They are sold as powders, drinks and capsules for skin, hair, nails, joints and bone. Collagen itself is a family of structural proteins that make up much of the extracellular matrix of connective tissue, rich in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline.[1][2] Proponents see a swallowed source of collagen-derived peptides as a way to support the skin's own structure from the inside.

The best-studied appearance claim concerns skin. Several randomised trials of oral collagen peptides report improvements in skin hydration, elasticity or wrinkles,[3][4][5][6][7] and early systematic reviews described largely consistent benefit.[8] A 2026 meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials of oral and topical peptides found significant improvement in hydration and brightness and a modest pooled effect on wrinkles, with inconsistent effects on elasticity and density.[9] A 2025 meta-analysis in the American Journal of Medicine is reported to have found that skin benefits shrink or vanish in higher-quality and non-industry-funded trials.[10]

Wikipedia's collagen article states that there is no good evidence that ingesting collagen affects the body's own collagen production or skin health, and that ingested collagen is digested into peptides and amino acids rather than incorporated intact.[1] Trial authors and some reviewers describe direct effects of absorbed peptides on skin cells; others suggest the peptides act as a source of amino acids.[8] No hair-growth effect from collagen peptides alone has been reported, though they are frequently marketed for hair.[11]

paras: Wikipedia reports that 28 human collagen types had been identified as of 2011, with types I and III making up more than 90 percent of human collagen. Type I is found in skin, tendon and bone, type II is the main collagen of cartilage, and type III often appears alongside type I.[1]

Each collagen molecule is a triple helix of three polypeptide chains, with glycine at nearly every third position and proline making up around 17 percent of the sequence. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are modified after translation in a step that requires vitamin C, which is why collagen supplements are frequently sold with vitamin C.[1][5] The triple helical structure was proposed by G. N. Ramachandran in 1955.[1]

Heating collagen denatures it into gelatin, a protein long used in cooking and industry; gelatin has been made from animal skin, bones and connective tissue and hydrolysed further to give the low-molecular-weight peptides used in supplements.[26] Bone broth, a food rich in gelatinised collagen, was a health fad in the early 2010s, helped by the 2014 book Nourishing Broth.[27]

Marketed as nutricosmetics for skin ageing, hair and nails, collagen peptides are among the most commonly sold beauty supplements.[11] They are often combined with vitamin C, zinc or biotin, as in a drinkable product tested in 72 women aged 35 and older.[5]

In looksmaxxing and fitness communities they are discussed as a skin and anti-ageing aid, as an inexpensive protein add-on, and as a food-based joint and tendon support alongside training.[23][24][25]

Collagen peptides have also been investigated for bone mineral density in postmenopausal women,[12] muscle recovery and fatigue,[13] body composition and strength alongside resistance training in older men,[29] and in reviews of muscle hypertrophy supplements.[14] Marine collagen has been reviewed as a biomaterial for wound healing, skin anti-ageing and bone regeneration.[15]

Products are classed by animal source. Bovine and porcine collagen peptides come from hides, bones and skin; marine collagen peptides come from fish skin and scales. A review of marine collagen describes it as water soluble, metabolically compatible and readily available, and compares its advantages with land-animal sources.[15] The tested products in randomised trials include branded specific-peptide products, low-molecular-weight collagen peptides and multi-ingredient drinks.[3][5][6][7]

Gelatin hydrolysates and collagen peptides share a manufacturing basis; hydrolysed collagen sits within the long history of gelatin, which is made mainly from by-products of the meat and leather industries. Religious dietary rules such as halal and kosher affect which sources are acceptable to some consumers.[26]

After digestion, collagen peptides, particularly hydroxyproline-containing di- and tripeptides, are absorbed. A 2005 study in healthy volunteers who ingested gelatin hydrolysates from porcine skin, chicken feet and cartilage found that the peptide form of hydroxyproline increased significantly in blood after ingestion.[28] The 2020 mechanistic review described direct effects of the peptides on fibroblasts, effects on macrophages and other pathways.[8]

An alternative view is that they simply supply amino acids that the body uses like other protein.[1] Bioavailability studies of marine and bovine peptides are registered.[18][19] Research on collagen's role in inflammation and on synthetic collagen-mimetic peptides is ongoing.[21][22]

Skin: a 2020 mechanistic systematic review of 10 publications concluded that oral intact or hydrolysed collagen improved clinical skin-health measures and described three proposed mechanisms.[8] A 2014 randomised trial of specific bioactive collagen peptides reported reduced skin wrinkles and increased dermal matrix synthesis,[7] and a 2015 report combined an ex vivo model and trials on skin moisture and the dermal collagen network.[4] A 2019 randomised, placebo-controlled study of a drinkable supplement containing 2.5 g of collagen peptides with vitamin C, zinc and biotin in 72 women aged 35 and over reported improvements in hydration, elasticity, roughness and density.[5] Randomised trials of low-molecular-weight collagen peptides reported skin benefits in 2024 and 2025.[3][6]

Meta-analyses: a 2023 meta-analysis of oral collagen for skin anti-ageing and another of hydrolysed collagen for skin rejuvenation are available.[16][17] The 2026 meta-analysis of 19 trials with 1,341 participants reported significant improvement in hydration and brightness, modest wrinkle reduction (mean difference 0.27, p = 0.04), driven by oral polypeptides, and inconsistent elasticity and density effects, with minimal adverse events.[9] The 2025 American Journal of Medicine meta-analysis is described as finding attenuated benefit in higher-quality, non-industry-funded trials.[10] Many individual trials are funded by the manufacturers of the tested products.
Hair: no randomised trial of collagen peptides alone for hair growth has been published.

Other outcomes: a randomised trial of 131 postmenopausal women reported effects on bone mineral density and bone markers over 12 months,[12] a 2015 randomised trial reported improved body composition and strength with collagen peptides plus resistance training in older sarcopenic men,[29] an integrative review examined muscle damage recovery,[13] and registered trials examine bioavailability, skin health and plantar fasciitis.[18][19][20]

Trials report few adverse events.[9] Possible allergy to marine or bovine sources and contamination in lightly regulated supplements are general considerations discussed for nutricosmetics.[11][15] For gelatin, regulators have considered the risk of animal-origin diseases such as BSE, with the EU judging the risk from bovine bone gelatin very low, and some people have severe allergic reactions to gelatin in injected vaccines.[26]

Collagen peptides are among the most commonly sold beauty supplements, offered as powders, drinks and capsules, often with vitamin C and other micronutrients.[11] Wikipedia notes that cosmetics often use partially hydrolysed collagen or low-molecular-weight peptides on the belief that they are absorbed better, and that topical products with intact collagen are poorly absorbed.[1]

On looksmax.org a user reported taking large daily amounts of collagen peptides and noticing a difference in skin and a younger look, and replies compared its cost with whey protein.[23] T Nation members describe adding collagen with vitamin C before tendon-focused work, or suggest it as a lower-cost alternative to bone broth.[24][25] Wikipedia's article on stock reports that there is no scientific evidence supporting many of the claims made for bone broth.[27]
The European Food Safety Authority found in 2011 no established cause-and-effect link between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance, according to Wikipedia.[26]

lore.intro: Collagen peptides are discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a skin and anti-aging supplement, including very high daily doses, and on T Nation as a protein or connective-tissue add-on to training diets.[23][24][25]

claims.claim: Mega-dosing collagen peptides (100-140 g a day) visibly improves skin
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports taking about 130 g of collagen daily, says he noticed a difference in his skin and looked younger, and attributes this to higher intake raising the amount that reaches the skin to stimulate collagen and elastin.[23]
claims.experts: Randomised trials of oral collagen peptides have used much smaller daily amounts and reported improvements in skin hydration, elasticity or wrinkles, while a 2025 meta-analysis is reported to have found smaller effects in higher-quality and non-industry-funded trials.[4][5][7][10] The thread's poster states that no studies of 100 g or more daily had been done, and no trial has tested such doses.[23]

claims.claim: Collagen supplements are a 'cope' for skin
claims.believers: In replies to the mega-dosing thread, one user says he had thought collagen supplements were "cope", while the poster says the cost is comparable to whey and another asks whether collagen shakes should replace whey.[23]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of randomised trials report improved skin hydration and a modest effect on wrinkles, with inconsistent effects on elasticity and density, and a 2025 meta-analysis is reported to describe shrinking benefit in higher-quality trials.[9][10][16][17]

claims.claim: Eating collagen replaces the body's own collagen production
claims.believers: Nutricosmetic products are marketed for skin ageing, and users describe taking collagen to support the skin's own collagen.[11][23]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that ingested collagen is digested to peptides and amino acids and that there is no good evidence it affects collagen production; trial authors describe peptide signalling to fibroblasts as a proposed mechanism.[1][8]

claims.claim: Collagen peptides taken with vitamin C support tendons and connective tissue
claims.believers: A T Nation member describes trying collagen peptides again with vitamin C (20 g with 1000 mg), spacing the drink 45 minutes before loaded isometric tendon work in his training log.[24]
claims.experts: Collagen peptides have been studied in bone-density and muscle-damage-recovery research,[12][13] and vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation step in collagen formation;[1] no tendon-specific trial has been reported.

claims.claim: Collagen peptides are a cheaper substitute for bone broth
claims.believers: A T Nation reply to a lifter's post asks whether he has thought of replacing bone broth with collagen peptides, saying they would be a lot cheaper and that he uses ones made from beef, fish and eggs.[25]
claims.experts: Reviews describe collagen peptides as enzymatically hydrolysed animal collagen sold as powders and drinks, and bioavailability trials have measured peptide absorption from such products; no comparison with bone broth has been reported.[1][18][19]

claims.believers: Collagen is routinely marketed for hair, skin and nails together.[11]
claims.experts: No randomised trial of collagen peptides alone for hair growth has been published.
